then.text: My lady, my lord, the mead is poured and the champion is sulking. A fine banquet. Come back any night.
Mead, bread and a harper! Then let the banquet begin. Be upstanding for the Earl of Thomond!
Tradition demands a guest be found guilty of some crime and thrown in the dungeon. Tonight's accused is... you. The crime: eating soup without a spoon. Unless you can best the Earl's champion.
Acquitted! The court rises. Mead all round, and a jug for our guest, and the Earl's thanks.
No forks at a medieval banquet, mind. A knife, your fingers and a great deal of confidence.

else.text: We have mead and bread. But a banquet without music is just a big dinner. Find the harpist in the Folk Park.
Mead, yes. Bread, no. The bean an tí in the Folk Park cottage bakes the best brown bread in Clare. Ask her nicely.
First, the mead. Durty Nelly's, over the bridge. Tell the barman the Butler sent you; he'll sigh, but he'll do it.
Welcome to Bunratty! I am the Butler. Tonight there is a medieval banquet in the Great Hall, as there has been most nights since the 1960s.
But I am short of three things: mead from Durty Nelly's, brown bread from the Folk Park, and a harpist. Could you fetch them? There'll be a seat at the high table in it.

bunratty_wench.text: We sing between courses. The songs are old and the jokes are older. Grace before meat is sung in Latin, mostly to stop people starting on the bread.
The tapestries are mostly from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Lord Gort bought the castle in 1954 and filled it with medieval furniture. Very good furniture. Nobody's allowed to sit on it.

bunratty_historian.text: There's been a fort on this spot since the Vikings had a trading post here. This castle is the fourth on the site, built around 1425.
The O'Briens took it in the 1500s and held it as Earls of Thomond. In 1646 Cromwell's side... well, Parliament's side, took it after a siege. The castle's seen a few dinners go badly.
